docs.title: KARIANA
docs.text:
AI-Powered Unreal Engine Control

Control Unreal Engine with natural language through 218+ MCP tools. Build, organize, and automate your game development workflow with Claude.

Get Started View on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
KARIANA is an AI-powered Unreal Engine 5.7+ plugin that enables comprehensive engine control through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Describe what you want in natural language, and Claude executes it in Unreal Engine.

Example

You: "Spawn a red cube at position 100, 0, 50 and add a point light above it"

Claude: Spawns the cube, creates a red material, applies it, and positions a point light - all automatically.

docs.title: 218+ MCP Tools
docs.text: Complete programmatic control of Unreal Engine with tools for actors, materials, blueprints, PCG, and more.

docs.title: Action Recorder
docs.text: Record your editor actions and generate reusable skills that can be replayed automatically.

docs.title: 22 Custom PCG Nodes
docs.text: Advanced procedural content generation with noise functions, patterns, and point manipulation.

docs.title: LLM Integration
docs.text: Built-in support for Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek, and XAI for AI-powered workflows.

docs.title: KARIANA-Anim
docs.text: Tweening system for smooth animations and runtime motion control.

docs.title: Spatial Patterns
docs.text: Grid, circular, spline, scatter, and surface-based spawning with expert pattern selection.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: Common questions about KARIANA.

docs.title: What is KARIANA?
docs.text: KARIANA is an AI-powered plugin that connects Claude (or other AI assistants) to Unreal Engine, allowing natural language control of the engine. Instead of clicking through menus, you describe what you want and it happens.

docs.title: What can I do with KARIANA?
docs.text:
• Spawn and manipulate actors
  • Create and apply materials
  • Set up lighting
  • Create Blueprints
  • Organize your level
  • Take screenshots
  • And 200+ more operations

docs.title: Which Unreal Engine versions are supported?
docs.text: KARIANA requires Unreal Engine 5.7 or newer.

docs.title: Which AI assistants work with KARIANA?
docs.text: Currently, Claude Desktop is the primary supported client. Any MCP-compatible client should work.

docs.title: Is KARIANA free?
docs.text: Yes, KARIANA is open source and free to use.

docs.title: Where do I install the plugin?
docs.text:
Two options:

  1. Engine-wide: [UE Install]/Engine/Plugins/Marketplace/KARIANA/
  2. Per-project: [Your Project]/Plugins/KARIANA/

docs.title: The installer failed. What do I do?
docs.text:
Try manual installation:

  1. Download from GitHub Releases
  2. Extract to your plugins folder
  3. Enable in Edit > Plugins
  4. Configure Claude Desktop manually

See Installation Guide for details.

docs.title: Do I need to install anything else?
docs.text:
Yes, enable these UE plugins:

  • Remote Control API
  • Remote Control Web Interface
  • Python Script Plugin

docs.title: How do I talk to Unreal Engine?
docs.text:
Just describe what you want in natural language:

"Spawn a red cube at 0, 0, 100"
"Add a spotlight above the cube"
"Take a screenshot"

docs.title: Do I need to know tool names?
docs.text: No! Just describe your intent. KARIANA figures out which tools to use.

docs.title: Can I undo KARIANA's changes?
docs.text: Yes, use Unreal Engine's standard undo (Ctrl+Z). Most KARIANA operations are undoable.

docs.title: Can I use KARIANA while the game is playing?
docs.text: Most features work during Play In Editor (PIE). Some editor-only features may be limited.

docs.title: How do I stop a long operation?
docs.text: Close Claude Desktop or stop the operation in UE. KARIANA operations respect cancellation.

docs.title: Can KARIANA create entire games?
docs.text: KARIANA is a tool, not a game generator. It helps with specific tasks like level design, lighting, and prototyping. Creating a complete game requires human creativity and design.

docs.title: Does KARIANA support C++?
docs.text: KARIANA primarily works with editor operations. For C++ code generation, you'd use Claude directly, not through KARIANA.

docs.title: Can I use custom meshes?
docs.text:
Yes, reference them by their content path:

"Spawn an actor with mesh /Game/MyMeshes/Chair"

docs.title: Does KARIANA work with Marketplace assets?
docs.text: Yes, any asset in your project can be referenced.

docs.title: Can KARIANA create animations?
docs.text: Limited support through Sequencer tools. Full animation creation is not yet supported.

docs.title: Is KARIANA slow?
docs.text: Most operations complete in milliseconds. Complex operations (like building lighting) take as long as they would manually.

docs.title: Does KARIANA affect editor performance?
docs.text: Minimal impact. The socket server uses negligible resources when idle.

docs.title: Can I use KARIANA on large projects?
docs.text: Yes, but operations on many actors may take longer. Use batch operations and organization for best results.

docs.title: "UE_NOT_CONNECTED" error
docs.text:
1. Ensure Unreal Engine is running with a project open
  2. Check that Remote Control plugins are enabled
  3. Verify ports 30010 and 9877 aren't blocked

See Troubleshooting for more solutions.

docs.title: Claude can't find KARIANA tools
docs.text:
1. Check your Claude Desktop config file
  2. Verify JSON syntax
  3. Restart Claude Desktop completely

docs.title: Commands work but nothing happens
docs.text:
1. Check you're in the right level
  2. Verify actor names are correct
  3. Look in Output Log for errors

docs.title: Is KARIANA safe to use?
docs.text: Yes. KARIANA only responds to local connections by default. It cannot be accessed remotely unless you explicitly configure it.

docs.title: Does KARIANA send data anywhere?
docs.text: No. All communication is local between Claude Desktop, the MCP server, and Unreal Engine.

docs.title: Can KARIANA delete my files?
docs.text: KARIANA only operates within Unreal Engine. It can delete assets within UE but not arbitrary files on your system.

docs.title: Can I extend KARIANA?
docs.text: Yes! KARIANA is open source. You can add custom tools by modifying the Python handlers.

docs.title: How do I report bugs?
docs.text:
Open an issue on GitHub with:

  • Steps to reproduce
  • Expected vs actual behavior
  • UE and KARIANA versions

docs.title: Can I contribute?
docs.text: Yes! See the Contributing Guide.

docs.title: How is KARIANA different from Unreal's AI features?
docs.text: Unreal's built-in AI features focus on runtime game AI (behavior trees, etc.). KARIANA is for editor-time operations controlled by an external AI assistant.

docs.title: Why use KARIANA instead of Blueprints?
docs.text:
Different use cases:

  • Blueprints: Permanent game logic
  • KARIANA: Rapid prototyping, level design, bulk operations

They complement each other.

docs.title: Can KARIANA replace a level designer?
docs.text: No. KARIANA is a tool that helps level designers work faster. Human creativity and design sense are still essential.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Solutions for common KARIANA issues.

docs.title: "UE_NOT_CONNECTED" Error
docs.text:
Symptoms: Claude reports it cannot connect to Unreal Engine.

Solutions:

  1. Verify UE is running
  2. Open Unreal Engine
  3. Load or create a project

  4. Check that the editor is fully loaded

  5. Check Remote Control plugin

  6. Go to Edit > Plugins
  7. Search for "Remote Control"
  8. Ensure both plugins are enabled

  9. Restart UE if you just enabled them

  10. Verify ports 

    # Check if ports are listening (Windows)
netstat -an | findstr "30010"
netstat -an | findstr "9877"

  11. Check firewall

  12. Allow UE through Windows Firewall

  13. Allow ports 30010, 30020, 9877

  14. Restart services

  15. Close Claude Desktop
  16. Close Unreal Engine
  17. Restart both

docs.title: "Connection Refused"
docs.text:
Symptoms: Socket connection fails immediately.

Solutions:

  1. Check KARIANA plugin is enabled
  2. Edit > Plugins > KARIANA

  3. Enable and restart

  4. Verify socket server started

  5. Check Output Log for: [KARIANA] Socket server started

  6. Check port availability 

    netstat -an | findstr "9877"
    If another app uses 9877, change the port in settings.

docs.title: Intermittent Disconnections
docs.text:
Symptoms: Connection works sometimes, drops randomly.

Solutions:

  1. Increase timeout 

    {
  "env": {
    "KARIANA_TIMEOUT": "60"
  }
}

  2. Check system resources

  3. Close unnecessary applications

  4. Check CPU/memory usage

  5. Disable sleep mode

  6. Prevent computer from sleeping during use

docs.title: "Actor Not Found"
docs.text:
Symptoms: Commands fail with actor not found error.

Solutions:

  1. Use exact name 

    "Select the actor named 'Cube_1'" (not just 'Cube')

  2. Check World Outliner

  3. Verify the actor exists

  4. Note the exact name

  5. Refresh actor list 

    "List all actors in the level"

docs.title: "Material Not Applied"
docs.text:
Symptoms: Material command succeeds but object doesn't change.

Solutions:

  1. Verify actor has mesh

  2. Empty actors can't have materials

  3. Check material exists 

    "List all materials"

  4. Specify material slot 

    "Apply M_Red to element 0 of the cube"

docs.title: "Blueprint Compilation Failed"
docs.text:
Symptoms: Blueprint operations fail to compile.

Solutions:

  1. Check for errors 

    "Check BP_MyActor for compilation errors"

  2. Verify nodes are connected

  3. Execution pins must be connected

  4. Check variable types

  5. Ensure type compatibility

docs.title: Slow Response Times
docs.text:
Symptoms: Commands take long to execute.

Solutions:

  1. Reduce actor count
  2. Many actors slow down operations

  3. Organize into folders

  4. Disable real-time rendering

  5. Window > Viewports > Realtime off

  6. Close unnecessary editor tabs

  7. Check background processes

docs.title: High Memory Usage
docs.text:
Symptoms: UE or system runs out of memory.

Solutions:

  1. Restart UE periodically

  2. Clear undo history

  3. Edit > Editor Preferences > Undo

  4. Reduce undo buffer size

  5. Purge unused assets

  6. Content Browser > right-click > Asset Actions > Fix Up Redirectors

docs.title: Plugin Not Visible
docs.text:
Symptoms: KARIANA doesn't appear in plugins list.

Solutions:

  1. Verify installation location
  2. Engine: [UE]/Engine/Plugins/Marketplace/KARIANA/

  3. Project: [Project]/Plugins/KARIANA/

  4. Check plugin file exists

  5. KARIANA.uplugin should be present

  6. Verify UE version

  7. KARIANA requires UE 5.7+

docs.title: Plugin Crashes UE
docs.text:
Symptoms: Unreal Engine crashes when plugin loads.

Solutions:

  1. Check dependencies
  2. Enable Remote Control first

  3. Enable Python Script Plugin

  4. Verify plugin integrity

  5. Re-download and reinstall

  6. Check logs

  7. [Project]/Saved/Logs/
  8. Look for crash info

docs.title: "No Tools Available"
docs.text:
Symptoms: Claude doesn't see KARIANA tools.

Solutions:

  1. Check config file location

  2. Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

  3. Verify JSON syntax 

    # Validate JSON
python -m json.tool claude_desktop_config.json

  4. Restart Claude Desktop

  5. Fully close (check system tray)

  6. Reopen

  7. Check MCP logs

  8. View > Developer > MCP Logs

docs.title: MCP Server Won't Start
docs.text:
Symptoms: Server process fails to launch.

Solutions:

  1. Check Python installation 

    python --version
uvx --version

  2. Install dependencies 

    pip install kariana-mcp

  3. Check command path

  4. Verify uvx or python is in PATH

docs.text: Error Cause Solution TIMEOUT Operation took too long Increase timeout, simplify request INVALID_PARAMS Wrong parameter types Check tool documentation PERMISSION_DENIED Operation not allowed Check context (editor vs PIE) ASSET_NOT_FOUND Asset path incorrect Verify path in Content Browser SOCKET_ERROR Network issue Check ports, restart services

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Get KARIANA up and running in minutes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before beginning, ensure you have:

  • Unreal Engine 5.7 or newer
  • Claude Desktop application
  • Windows 10/11 (macOS/Linux coming soon)

docs.title: Quick Install (Recommended)
docs.text:
Open PowerShell and run:

irm kariana.ai/install.ps1 | iex

The installer automatically:

  1. Locates your Unreal Engine installation
  2. Installs the KARIANA plugin
  3. Configures Claude Desktop
  4. Verifies the connection

That's it!

After the installer completes, you're ready to use KARIANA.

docs.title: Manual Installation
docs.text: If you prefer manual setup or the quick install doesn't work:

docs.title: Step 1: Download the Plugin
docs.text: Download the latest release from GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Step 2: Install the Plugin
docs.text:
Extract the zip and copy the KARIANA folder to your Unreal Engine plugins directory:

Engine-wide InstallationProject-specific Installation 
C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.7\Engine\Plugins\Marketplace\KARIANA

YourProject\Plugins\KARIANA

Using Symlinks

For development, use a symbolic link to keep the plugin synced with your git repository:

# Run as Administrator
mklink /D "C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.7\Engine\Plugins\Marketplace\KARIANA" "D:\path\to\KARIANA"

docs.title: Step 3: Enable Required Plugins
docs.text:
In Unreal Engine, go to Edit > Plugins and enable:

  • Remote Control
  • Python Script Plugin
  • KARIANA

Restart Unreal Engine when prompted.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Claude Desktop
docs.text:
1. Open Claude Desktop
  2. Go to Settings > Developer > MCP Servers
  3. Add this configuration:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kariana-plugin": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["kariana-mcp-server"]
    }
  }
}
  1. Restart Claude Desktop

docs.title: Check Unreal Engine
docs.text:
Open Window > Developer Tools > Output Log and look for:

[KARIANA] Socket server started on port 9877
[KARIANA] MCP server ready

docs.title: Check Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Ask Claude:

"What Unreal MCP tools do you have available?"

Claude should list tools like control_actor, manage_asset, etc.

docs.title: Test Command
docs.text:
Try a simple command:

"Spawn a cube in Unreal Engine at position 0, 0, 100"

A cube should appear in your level!

docs.title: Understanding MCP
docs.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standardized interface that allows Claude to interact with external tools like KARIANA.

docs.title: What is MCP?
docs.text:
Think of MCP as a universal remote control for AI assistants. Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, MCP provides a standard way for AI to:

  • Discover available tools
  • Understand what each tool does
  • Call tools with the right parameters
  • Receive and process results

Analogy

MCP is like USB for AI tools - a universal standard that lets different devices (tools) work with different computers (AI models).

docs.title: How Claude Uses MCP
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Your Request] --> B{Claude}
    B --> C[Select Tool]
    C --> D[Call with Parameters]
    D --> E[KARIANA Executes]
    E --> F[Return Results]
    F --> B
    B --> G[Report to You]
  1. You make a request in natural language
  2. Claude selects the appropriate tool(s)
  3. Claude calls the tool with parameters
  4. Tool executes in Unreal Engine
  5. Results return to Claude
  6. Claude reports what happened

docs.title: Example Flow
docs.text:
Your request:

"Spawn a red cube at position 100, 0, 50"

What Claude does:

  1. Determines needed tools: control_actor (spawn), manage_asset (material), control_actor (apply)
  2. Calls control_actor to spawn a cube
  3. Calls manage_asset to create a red material
  4. Calls control_actor to apply the material
  5. Reports success

docs.title: Two Communication Channels
docs.text: KARIANA uses two separate channels for maximum capability:

docs.title: External MCP Server
docs.text:
Uses Unreal's built-in Remote Control plugin.

Property Value Protocol HTTP + WebSocket Ports 30010 (HTTP), 30020 (WS) Tools 50+ core actions Use cases Asset management, actor control, editor commands

docs.title: Plugin Socket Server
docs.text:
Uses KARIANA's direct plugin connection.

Property Value Protocol TCP Socket Port 9877 Tools 168 specialized features Use cases Blueprints, PCG, world organization, advanced features

Automatic Selection

You don't need to know which channel to use - KARIANA automatically routes commands to the right channel.

docs.title: Core Tools (External MCP)
docs.text: Tool Purpose control_actor Spawn, move, delete actors manage_asset List, import, create assets control_editor Play, stop, camera control manage_level Level operations, streaming create_effect Particles, debug visualization

docs.title: Advanced Tools (Plugin)
docs.text: Tool Purpose manage_blueprint Blueprint creation and editing build_environment Landscape, foliage world_organizer Automatic organization pcg_tools Procedural generation quick_actions Light creation, alignment

docs.title: Natural Language Tips
docs.text:
You don't need to know tool names. Just describe what you want:

Good Requests

  • "Create a cube"
  • "Add a red material to the sphere"
  • "Put 5 spotlights in a circle around the actor"

Less Effective

  • "Use control_actor spawn"
  • "Call manage_asset create_material"

Be specific for better results:

Instead of... Try... "Make it look nice" "Add a gold metallic material with 0.2 roughness" "Some lights" "Add 3 point lights with warm color (3000K)" "Move it" "Move the cube 500 units along the X axis"

docs.title: What is KARIANA?
docs.text: KARIANA functions as a connection layer between AI assistants like Claude and Unreal Engine, enabling natural language control of the engine without manual interface navigation or coding.

docs.title: The Simple Explanation
docs.text:
You can issue commands such as "Spawn a red cube in the middle of the level" and have them execute directly in Unreal Engine. No menus, no code, no complexity.

Think of it like...

Having a skilled Unreal Engine developer who instantly understands and executes your creative vision.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant You
    participant Claude
    participant KARIANA
    participant Unreal Engine

    You->>Claude: "Spawn a red cube at 0, 0, 100"
    Claude->>KARIANA: Translates to MCP tool calls
    KARIANA->>Unreal Engine: Executes commands
    Unreal Engine->>KARIANA: Returns results
    KARIANA->>Claude: Sends response
    Claude->>You: "Done! Created cube with red material"
  1. You request an action from Claude in natural language
  2. Claude translates your request into MCP tool calls
  3. KARIANA sends commands to Unreal Engine
  4. Unreal Engine executes the commands
  5. Results flow back through KARIANA to Claude
  6. Claude confirms what was done

  • Non-programmer access - Everyone can contribute
  • Reduced coordination - Direct engine access
  • Command documentation - Natural language is self-documenting

docs.title: What Can You Do?
docs.text:
Here are some examples of what you can ask:

"Spawn 10 cubes in a row along the X axis, 200 units apart"

"Create a gold material with high metallic and low roughness"

"Add a spotlight facing the player start position"

"Take a screenshot from the current camera angle"

"Organize all the lights in the level into a folder called 'Lighting'"

"Create a Blueprint actor with a static mesh component"

docs.text:
Ready to get started?

Install KARIANA

docs.title: Tutorial: Create Materials
docs.text: Learn to create and apply materials to bring your scenes to life.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Creating colored materials
  • Setting material properties
  • Applying materials to actors
  • Material recipes for common looks

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Completed Spawn Your First Actor tutorial
  • Some actors in your level to apply materials to

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Simple Color Material
docs.text:
Start with a basic red material:

"Create a red material called M_Red"

This creates a material with red base color.

docs.title: Step 2: Apply the Material
docs.text:
Apply it to an actor:

"Spawn a cube at 0, 0, 100"
"Apply M_Red to the cube"

The cube should now be red!

docs.title: Step 3: Create with Properties
docs.text:
Let's make a more interesting material:

"Create a material called M_Gold with:
- Base color: gold (255, 200, 50)
- Metallic: 1.0
- Roughness: 0.2"

Apply it:

"Spawn a sphere at 200, 0, 100"
"Apply M_Gold to the sphere"

docs.title: Step 4: Material Property Guide
docs.text: Property Range Effect Metallic 0-1 0=plastic, 1=metal Roughness 0-1 0=mirror, 1=matte Specular 0-1 Highlight brightness

docs.title: Try These Combinations
docs.text:
Shiny Plastic: 

"Create M_ShinyPlastic: blue color, metallic 0, roughness 0.1"

Brushed Metal: 

"Create M_BrushedMetal: silver color, metallic 1, roughness 0.4"

Matte Rubber: 

"Create M_Rubber: black color, metallic 0, roughness 0.9"

docs.title: Step 5: Emissive Materials
docs.text:
Create glowing materials:

"Create a material called M_Glow with:
- Base color: cyan
- Emissive color: cyan
- Emissive intensity: 5"

This material will appear to glow!

docs.title: Step 6: Transparent Materials
docs.text:
Create glass-like materials:

"Create a material called M_Glass with:
- Base color: light blue
- Opacity: 0.3
- Blend mode: translucent"

Note

Transparent materials require the blend mode to be set to translucent.

docs.title: Step 7: Material Showcase
docs.text:
Create a showcase of different materials:

"Spawn 5 spheres in a row at Y=0, Z=100, from X=-400 to X=400"

Then apply different materials:

"Apply M_Red to the first sphere"
"Apply M_Gold to the second sphere"
"Apply M_ShinyPlastic to the third sphere"
"Apply M_BrushedMetal to the fourth sphere"
"Apply M_Glow to the fifth sphere"

docs.title: Step 8: Quick Material Application
docs.text:
Apply materials directly without creating first:

"Make the cube blue"
"Give the sphere a gold metallic look"
"Make the cylinder look like chrome"

KARIANA will create and apply the material automatically.

docs.title: Chrome
docs.text: "Create M_Chrome: silver color, metallic 1, roughness 0.05"

docs.title: Copper
docs.text: "Create M_Copper: RGB(184,115,51), metallic 1, roughness 0.3"

docs.title: Plastic (Colored)
docs.text: "Create M_PlasticRed: red color, metallic 0, roughness 0.5"

docs.title: Wood-like
docs.text: "Create M_Wood: RGB(139,90,43), metallic 0, roughness 0.8"

docs.title: Neon
docs.text: "Create M_Neon: pink color, emissive pink at intensity 10"

docs.title: Challenge: Material Gallery
docs.text:
Create a gallery showcasing 6 different material types:

  1. Matte plastic
  2. Glossy plastic
  3. Brushed metal
  4. Polished metal
  5. Emissive/glowing
  6. Transparent
Solution 
"Create material gallery:

Spawn 6 spheres in a 2x3 grid at Z=100, spacing 300 units

Create and apply:
- M_MattePlastic (red, metallic 0, roughness 0.8) to sphere 1
- M_GlossyPlastic (blue, metallic 0, roughness 0.1) to sphere 2
- M_BrushedMetal (silver, metallic 1, roughness 0.5) to sphere 3
- M_PolishedMetal (gold, metallic 1, roughness 0.05) to sphere 4
- M_NeonGlow (cyan, emissive cyan intensity 5) to sphere 5
- M_Glass (white, opacity 0.2, translucent) to sphere 6"

docs.title: Tutorial: Lighting Setup
docs.text: Learn to illuminate your scenes with professional lighting techniques.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Adding different light types
  • Three-point lighting setup
  • Light properties and colors
  • Creating mood with lighting

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Some actors in your level
  • Materials applied (optional but recommended)

docs.title: Step 1: Add Your First Light
docs.text:
Start with a simple point light:

"Add a point light at 0, 0, 300"

This adds an omnidirectional light above the origin.

docs.title: Step 2: Adjust Light Properties
docs.text:
Make it brighter and warmer:

"Set the point light intensity to 5000"
"Set the light color to warm white (3000 Kelvin)"

docs.title: Step 3: Add a Spotlight
docs.text:
Create focused lighting:

"Add a spotlight at 500, 0, 400 pointing at the origin"

Adjust the cone:

"Set the spotlight outer cone angle to 45 degrees"
"Set intensity to 8000"

docs.title: Step 4: Three-Point Lighting
docs.text: The classic setup for showcasing objects:

docs.title: Key Light (Main Light)
docs.text:
"Add a spotlight called 'KeyLight' at 500, -300, 400"
"Point it at 0, 0, 100"
"Set intensity to 10000"
"Set color temperature to 5500K"

docs.title: Fill Light (Softer, Opposite Side)
docs.text:
"Add a point light called 'FillLight' at -400, 200, 300"
"Set intensity to 3000"
"Set color temperature to 6000K"

docs.title: Back Light (Rim/Separation)
docs.text:
"Add a spotlight called 'BackLight' at 0, 500, 350"
"Point it at 0, 0, 100"
"Set intensity to 6000"
"Set outer cone to 30 degrees"

docs.title: Step 5: Ambient Light
docs.text:
Add overall illumination with a sky light:

"Add a sky light"
"Set sky light intensity to 1.0"

This fills in the shadows.

docs.title: Step 6: Directional Light (Sunlight)
docs.text:
For outdoor scenes:

"Add a directional light for sunlight"
"Rotate it to point down at 45 degrees"
"Set intensity to 10 lux"
"Set color to daylight (5500K)"

docs.title: Step 7: Colored Lighting
docs.text:
Create mood with colored lights:

"Add a point light at 300, 0, 200 with blue color"
"Add a point light at -300, 0, 200 with orange color"

docs.title: Color Temperature Reference
docs.text: Temperature Color Mood 2700K Warm orange Cozy, intimate 3200K Warm white Indoor residential 4000K Neutral Office, commercial 5500K Daylight Natural outdoor 6500K Cool blue Bright, clinical

docs.title: Step 8: Light Attenuation
docs.text:
Control how far light reaches:

"Set the point light attenuation radius to 500"

Smaller radius = more focused light.

docs.title: Step 9: Shadows
docs.text:
Enable and configure shadows:

"Enable shadows on the key light"
"Set shadow resolution to high"

For soft shadows: 

"Set source radius to 50 for soft shadows"

docs.title: Studio Lighting
docs.text:
"Create studio lighting setup:
- Key light (spotlight) front-right, high, pointing at center
- Fill light (point) front-left, medium height
- Back light (spotlight) behind, pointing at subject
- White floor for bounce"

docs.title: Dramatic Scene
docs.text:
"Create dramatic lighting:
- Single strong spotlight from above
- No fill light
- Deep shadows
- Slight blue ambient"

docs.title: Warm Interior
docs.text:
"Create cozy interior:
- Warm point lights (2700K) at ceiling positions
- Rect lights for windows (5500K)
- Low intensity sky light for ambient"

docs.title: Challenge: Light a Scene
docs.text:
Light this simple scene effectively:

  1. Floor plane
  2. Three objects (cube, sphere, cylinder)
  3. Create appealing lighting
Solution 
"Set up the scene:
- Spawn floor: plane at 0,0,0 scaled 10,10,1
- Spawn cube at -200,0,75
- Spawn sphere at 0,0,100
- Spawn cylinder at 200,0,75

Apply materials:
- Red to cube
- Gold metallic to sphere
- Blue to cylinder

Add lighting:
- Key: spotlight at 400,-400,500 pointing at 0,0,100, intensity 12000, 5000K
- Fill: point light at -300,300,300, intensity 4000, 5500K
- Back: spotlight at 0,600,400 pointing at 0,0,100, intensity 5000
- Ambient: sky light at intensity 0.5"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Solution Scene too dark Increase light intensity, add more lights Harsh shadows Increase source radius, add fill light Flat looking Add contrast, use key/fill ratio Colors look wrong Check color temperature, add color grading

docs.title: Tutorial: Organize Your Level
docs.text: Learn to keep your levels clean and navigable with proper organization.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Creating folder structures
  • Organizing actors by type
  • Naming conventions
  • Using auto-organization

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A level with multiple actors
  • Completed previous tutorials (or have a messy level to organize)

docs.title: Step 1: View Current State
docs.text:
First, see what you have:

"List all actors in the level"

Or:

"Show the current World Outliner hierarchy"

docs.title: Step 2: Create Basic Folders
docs.text:
Set up a folder structure:

"Create folders: Environment, Lighting, Gameplay"

docs.title: Step 3: Organize by Type
docs.text:
Move actors to appropriate folders:

"Move all static meshes to the Environment folder"
"Move all lights to the Lighting folder"
"Move all triggers to Gameplay"

docs.title: Step 4: Create Subfolders
docs.text:
Add more organization:

"Create subfolder 'Props' inside Environment"
"Create subfolder 'Architecture' inside Environment"
"Create subfolders 'Key', 'Fill', 'Ambient' inside Lighting"

docs.title: Step 5: Rename Actors
docs.text:
Apply consistent naming:

"Rename all point lights to 'PointLight_##' with sequential numbers"
"Rename all cubes with prefix 'SM_Cube_'"

docs.title: Step 6: Auto-Organization
docs.text:
Let KARIANA organize automatically:

"Auto-organize all actors by type"

This creates a structure like: 

Level
├── Static Meshes
│   ├── Cubes
│   ├── Spheres
│   └── Others
├── Lights
│   ├── Point Lights
│   ├── Spot Lights
│   └── Directional Lights
└── Cameras

docs.title: Step 7: Tag Important Actors
docs.text:
Add tags for quick finding:

"Tag all interactive objects with 'Interactive'"
"Tag the main light as 'KeyLight'"

Find them later:

"Select all actors tagged 'Interactive'"

docs.title: Step 8: Clean Up
docs.text:
Remove clutter:

"Remove all empty folders"
"Delete actors named 'Untitled' or 'Default'"

docs.title: By Function
docs.text:
"Create organization structure:
- Gameplay
  - PlayerStart
  - Spawners
  - Triggers
  - Interactables
- Environment
  - Architecture
  - Props
  - Vegetation
- Lighting
  - Key Lights
  - Fill Lights
  - Ambient
- VFX
- Audio"

docs.title: By Area
docs.text:
"Create area-based organization:
- Area_Entrance
- Area_MainHall
- Area_Corridor
- Area_Exit
Each with Meshes, Lights, Gameplay subfolders"

docs.title: Naming Convention Reference
docs.text: Type Prefix Example Static Mesh SM_ SM_Chair_01 Blueprint BP_ BP_Door_Main Material M_ M_Wood_Oak Light L_ L_Point_01 Trigger T_ T_Entrance

docs.title: Step 9: Verify Organization
docs.text:
Check your work:

"Show the complete folder hierarchy"
"List any actors not in folders"
"Find duplicate named actors"

docs.title: As You Work
docs.text:
"Spawn a cube in the Environment/Props folder"
"Create light in Lighting/Fill"

docs.title: Regular Cleanup
docs.text:
"Move any unfiled actors to appropriate folders"
"Clean up empty folders"
"Check for naming convention violations"

docs.title: Challenge: Organize a Messy Level
docs.text:
Start with this messy setup:

"Spawn 10 random cubes at random positions"
"Spawn 5 point lights at random positions"
"Spawn 3 spotlights at random positions"
"Spawn 2 cameras at random positions"

Now organize it properly!

Solution 
"Organize the level:

Create folder structure:
- Environment/Props
- Lighting/Points
- Lighting/Spots
- Cameras

Move actors:
- All cubes to Environment/Props
- All point lights to Lighting/Points
- All spotlights to Lighting/Spots
- All cameras to Cameras

Rename:
- Cubes to 'Prop_Cube_##'
- Point lights to 'L_Point_##'
- Spotlights to 'L_Spot_##'
- Cameras to 'Cam_##'"

docs.title: Tutorial: Spawn Your First Actor
docs.text: Learn the basics of spawning actors with KARIANA.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Spawning basic shapes
  • Positioning actors
  • Applying transforms
  • Naming conventions

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• KARIANA installed and connected
  • Unreal Engine running with an empty level

docs.title: Step 1: Spawn a Simple Cube
docs.text:
Start with the most basic command:

"Spawn a cube"

You should see a cube appear at the world origin (0, 0, 0).

Check

Look in the World Outliner - you should see "Cube" or "StaticMeshActor".

docs.title: Step 2: Spawn with Position
docs.text:
Now let's control where the cube appears:

"Spawn a cube at position 500, 0, 100"

This places a cube at: - X: 500 (forward) - Y: 0 (center) - Z: 100 (up)

docs.title: Step 3: Add Rotation
docs.text:
Spawn a rotated cube:

"Spawn a cube at 0, 500, 100 rotated 45 degrees on the Z axis"

The cube should be tilted.

docs.title: Step 4: Apply Scale
docs.text:
Create a stretched cube:

"Spawn a cube at 0, 0, 200 with scale 2, 1, 0.5"

This creates: - 2x size on X (wide) - 1x size on Y (normal) - 0.5x size on Z (flat)

docs.title: Step 5: Full Transform
docs.text:
Combine everything:

"Spawn a cube at position 300, 300, 50, rotated 30 degrees on Z, scaled to 1.5, 1.5, 2"

docs.title: Step 6: Spawn Different Shapes
docs.text:
Try other basic shapes:

"Spawn a sphere at 0, 0, 300"
"Spawn a cylinder at 500, 0, 50"
"Spawn a cone at -500, 0, 50"

docs.title: Step 7: Batch Spawning
docs.text:
Create multiple objects at once:

"Spawn 5 cubes in a row along the X axis, 200 units apart, starting at 0, 0, 100"

You should see 5 cubes at: - (0, 0, 100) - (200, 0, 100) - (400, 0, 100) - (600, 0, 100) - (800, 0, 100)

docs.title: Step 8: Named Actors
docs.text:
Give your actors meaningful names:

"Spawn a cube named 'Floor' at 0, 0, 0 with scale 10, 10, 0.1"
"Spawn a sphere named 'Ball' at 0, 0, 100"

docs.title: Challenge: Build a Simple Scene
docs.text:
Try building this scene:

  1. A floor (flat cube, scaled wide)
  2. Four pillars (tall cubes at corners)
  3. A roof (flat cube on top)
  4. A sphere in the center
Solution 
"Create a simple temple:
- Floor: cube at 0,0,0 scaled 10,10,0.5
- Pillar 1: cube at 400,400,250 scaled 0.5,0.5,5
- Pillar 2: cube at -400,400,250 scaled 0.5,0.5,5
- Pillar 3: cube at 400,-400,250 scaled 0.5,0.5,5
- Pillar 4: cube at -400,-400,250 scaled 0.5,0.5,5
- Roof: cube at 0,0,500 scaled 12,12,0.5"

docs.title: Tutorial: Take Screenshots
docs.text: Learn to capture professional screenshots of your Unreal Engine work.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Basic screenshot capture
  • Camera positioning
  • High-resolution captures
  • Composition techniques

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A scene with actors, materials, and lighting
  • Completed previous tutorials (or any interesting scene)

docs.title: Step 1: Basic Screenshot
docs.text:
The simplest capture:

"Take a screenshot"

This captures the current viewport exactly as you see it.

Default Location

Screenshots save to [Project]/Saved/Screenshots/

docs.title: Step 2: Position the Camera
docs.text:
Get a better angle:

"Move the camera to 0, -500, 200 looking at the origin"

Then capture:

"Take a screenshot"

docs.title: Step 3: Frame Your Subject
docs.text:
Focus on a specific object:

"Frame the cube in the viewport"

Or look at a specific point:

"Point the camera at position 100, 0, 50"

docs.title: Step 4: Adjust Field of View
docs.text:
Change the lens:

"Set viewport FOV to 60"
FOV Effect Use Case 30-50 Narrow, compressed Portraits 60-75 Normal General 90-120 Wide, dramatic Environments

docs.title: Step 5: High Resolution
docs.text:
Capture at higher quality:

"Take a 4K screenshot"

Or specify exact resolution:

"Take a screenshot at 3840x2160"

docs.title: Step 6: Named Screenshots
docs.text:
Organize your captures:

"Take a screenshot named 'FinalScene_Front'"
"Take a screenshot named 'FinalScene_Top'"

docs.title: Step 7: Multiple Angles
docs.text:
Capture a turntable:

"Take screenshots from 8 angles around the center object, 45 degrees apart"

Or specific views:

"Take screenshot from front view, name it 'Front'"
"Take screenshot from left view, name it 'Left'"
"Take screenshot from top view, name it 'Top'"
"Take screenshot from a 45-degree angle, name it 'Hero'"

docs.title: Step 8: Clean Captures
docs.text:
Remove UI elements:

"Take a screenshot without UI"
"Capture viewport only, hide all overlays"

docs.title: Rule of Thirds
docs.text: "Position camera so the main subject is at the right third of the frame"

docs.title: Leading Lines
docs.text: "Frame the shot to use the floor lines leading to the subject"

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
"Add foreground elements for depth"
"Enable depth of field, focus on the subject"

docs.title: Enable High Quality
docs.text:
"Set viewport quality to cinematic"
"Enable ray tracing for screenshot"

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
"Add slight bloom for the screenshot"
"Enable color grading"

docs.title: Product Shot
docs.text:
"Product shot workflow:
1. Position object at center
2. Set up three-point lighting
3. Use neutral background
4. Camera at 45-degree angle
5. FOV 50 for minimal distortion
6. Take 4K screenshot"

docs.title: Environment Shot
docs.text:
"Environment shot workflow:
1. Find interesting composition
2. Use wide FOV (90)
3. Low camera angle for drama
4. Ensure good lighting coverage
5. Take screenshot at high res"

docs.title: All Cameras
docs.text: "Take a screenshot from each camera actor in the level"

docs.title: Documentation Set
docs.text:
"Create documentation screenshots:
- Wide establishing shot
- Detail shots of key features
- Top-down layout view
- Each named appropriately"

docs.title: Challenge: Photo Session
docs.text:
Create a professional photo session of a simple scene:

  1. Set up a scene with 3 objects
  2. Add proper lighting
  3. Take 5 different shots:
  4. Hero shot (main angle)
  5. Close-up detail
  6. Wide environment
  7. Top-down
  8. Dramatic low angle
Solution 
"Photo session:

Scene setup:
- Spawn sphere at 0,0,100
- Apply gold metallic material
- Three-point lighting

Shot 1 - Hero:
- Camera at 300,-300,200 looking at 0,0,100
- FOV 60
- Take screenshot named 'Hero'

Shot 2 - Close-up:
- Camera at 100,-100,120 looking at 0,0,100
- FOV 40
- Take screenshot named 'CloseUp'

Shot 3 - Wide:
- Camera at 0,-800,300 looking at 0,0,100
- FOV 90
- Take screenshot named 'Wide'

Shot 4 - Top:
- Camera at 0,0,500 looking straight down
- Take screenshot named 'TopDown'

Shot 5 - Dramatic:
- Camera at 200,-200,50 looking up at 0,0,100
- FOV 70
- Take screenshot named 'Dramatic'"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Solution Dark screenshot Check lighting, increase intensity Blurry Disable motion blur, check focus Wrong size Specify exact resolution UI visible Use "without UI" option

docs.title: Your First Commands
docs.text: Let's start using KARIANA with some simple commands.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting, ensure:

  • Unreal Engine is running with a project open
  • KARIANA plugin is enabled
  • Claude Desktop is configured and connected

Verify Connection

Ask Claude: "Can you see my Unreal Engine?" - Claude should confirm the connection.

docs.title: Spawning Objects
docs.text:
The most basic operation - creating objects in your level:

"Spawn a cube"

This creates a cube at the world origin (0, 0, 0).

With position: 

"Spawn a sphere at position 500, 200, 100"

With rotation: 

"Spawn a cube at 0, 0, 100 rotated 45 degrees on the Z axis"

With scale: 

"Spawn a cube scaled to 2, 2, 0.5"

docs.title: Available Shapes
docs.text: Shape Command Cube "Spawn a cube" Sphere "Spawn a sphere" Cylinder "Spawn a cylinder" Cone "Spawn a cone" Plane "Spawn a plane"

docs.title: Adding Lights
docs.text:
"Add a point light at 0, 0, 300"

Light types: 

"Add a spotlight facing down at position 0, 0, 500"
"Add a directional light for sunlight"
"Create a rect light at 200, 0, 200"

docs.title: Moving Objects
docs.text:
"Move the cube to position 100, 200, 0"
"Move the sphere 500 units along the X axis"
"Rotate the cube 90 degrees on the Y axis"
"Scale the cylinder to 0.5 on all axes"

docs.title: Deleting Objects
docs.text:
"Delete the cube"
"Delete all spheres in the level"
"Delete the last spawned actor"

docs.title: Creating Materials
docs.text:
"Create a red material called M_Red"
"Create a blue metallic material"
"Create a material with roughness 0.2 and metallic 1.0"

docs.title: Applying Materials
docs.text:
"Apply the red material to the cube"
"Make the sphere gold colored"
"Apply M_Red to all cubes in the level"

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Scene
docs.text:
"Create a simple scene with:
- A floor plane at 0, 0, 0 scaled to 10, 10, 1
- A red cube on top of it
- A point light above the cube"

docs.title: Example 2: Material Test
docs.text:
"Spawn 5 spheres in a row along the X axis, 200 units apart.
Give each one a different material: red, green, blue, gold, and glass."

docs.title: Example 3: Lighting Setup
docs.text:
"Set up three-point lighting:
- Key light (bright) at front-right
- Fill light (dimmer) at front-left
- Back light for rim lighting"

docs.title: Be Specific
docs.text:
Good

"Spawn a cube at position 100, 0, 50 with scale 2, 2, 2"

Vague

"Put something somewhere"

docs.title: Use Descriptive Language
docs.text:
Good

"Create a warm golden material with high metallic (0.9) and low roughness (0.1)"

Vague

"Make it look nice and shiny"

docs.title: Reference Objects Clearly
docs.text:
Good

"Move the cube named 'PlayerSpawn' to position 0, 0, 100"

Ambiguous

"Move that thing over there"

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Problem Solution "Can't find actor" Use the exact name or spawn a new one Objects spawn at origin Specify the position explicitly Wrong object selected Be more specific with names Material doesn't apply Ensure the actor has a mesh component

docs.title: Using Tools
docs.text:
You don't need to know tool names - just describe what you want:

# Instead of:
"Use control_actor spawn with type cube at position 0, 0, 100"

# Just say:
"Spawn a cube at 0, 0, 100"

Claude automatically selects the right tools.
